To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The records of teaching observations (ROTOs), used by HEIs to record and assess trainee teachers’ performance, can be seen as boundary objects, used by different stakeholders in the ITT process, to communicate their perceptions of the quality of the trainee’s performance, and the extent to which they have achieved professional standards.

The use of records of teaching observations as boundary objects between different Communities of Practice (CoPs) in the context of ITT programmes for PCE, is a potentially useful way of addressing the tension between the need for trainee teachers’ performance to be evaluated, and the desire to encourage them to engage in critical reflection on their practice.

• Observations can be a useful tool in the development of trainee teachers, but they are only one part of the process of professional development • The process of recording observations, and the records themselves, can be used to facilitate the sharing of information between different communities of professional practice, and • The records can be used to support trainees’ professional development, but this depends on the way they are used, the context in which they are used, and on the attitudes and beliefs of those using them
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of records of teaching observations in initial teacher education.
how trainee teachers’ records of teaching observations are used as boundary objects in the different communities of practice that constitute ITT programmes for PCE.
the way in which records of observations are used by different communities of practice, and how this impacts on the professional identity of trainee teachers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observations were useful in that the trainee teacher was aware of their strengths and weaknesses, which could be used to improve their own practice.
the observations are a boundary object between the communities of practice.
the observations are not fit-for-purpose, and that the process of observation and feedback should be reviewed and reformed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that observations are not only a boundary object between trainee teachers and their mentors, but also between the two communities of practice, that of the HEIs and the LLS.

we have found a way of recording and reporting teaching observations that enables the different communities of practice involved in the training and assessment of teachers to work more effectively with each other, and with the trainees, to develop their practice and improve their teaching.
teaching observations are a boundary object between different communities of teacher educators and trainees.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the introduction of a new system for the grading of trainee teachers’ performance in the classroom, based on a set of criteria, has led to an increased focus on the ‘what’ of teaching rather than the ‘how’.

the records of teaching observations can be seen as boundary objects that are able to facilitate communication between different communities of practices (CoP) in the ITT programme, including those of the trainee teachers, their tutors, and the trainee teachers’ mentors.

the records of observation can be a boundary object, allowing different communities of practice to engage with the process and the outcomes in ways that are meaningful to them, and which can lead to productive conversations.
